name: Pop Culture Classics
description: Hear a public-domain tune and name the show, film or game that made it famous.
question: Which show, film or game made this tune famous?

cards.fact: “Korobeiniki”, a Russian folk song set to an 1861 poem by Nikolay Nekrasov, became “Music A” in Tetris for the Game Boy (1989).
Grieg’s “In the Hall of the Mountain King” (Peer Gynt, 1875) beeps along under every level of Manic Miner, the 1983 ZX Spectrum platformer.
Johann Strauss II’s “The Blue Danube” (1866) plays while Elite’s docking computer flies you into a space station — a nod to 2001: A Space Odyssey.
The galloping finale of Rossini’s William Tell Overture (1829) was the Lone Ranger’s theme on radio from 1933 and on television from 1949.
Rimsky-Korsakov’s “Flight of the Bumblebee” (1900) buzzed under The Green Hornet on radio from 1936, and in Al Hirt’s trumpet version on the 1966 TV series.
Scott Joplin’s ragtime hit “The Entertainer” (1902) was nearly forgotten until Marvin Hamlisch adapted it for The Sting (1973), sending it to the top of the charts.
Wagner’s “Ride of the Valkyries” (Die Walküre, 1856) blares from the helicopters in the attack scene of Apocalypse Now (1979).
The sunrise fanfare of Richard Strauss’s Also sprach Zarathustra (1896) opens 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) — and has meant “something epic” ever since.
Bach’s Toccata and Fugue in D minor (c. 1710), in Leopold Stokowski’s orchestral arrangement, is the first segment of Disney’s Fantasia (1940).
Offenbach’s “Galop infernal” (Orpheus in the Underworld, 1858) became the Can-can of the Moulin Rouge cabaret, and kicks up its heels again in Baz Luhrmann’s Moulin Rouge! (2001).
Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake (1877) is the ballet Natalie Portman’s dancer is cast in — and unravels inside — in Black Swan (2010).
Pachelbel’s Canon in D (c. 1680) was obscure until it became the theme of Ordinary People (1980), which launched it into countless weddings.
Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony (1824) is the obsession of Alex — “lovely, lovely Ludwig van” — in A Clockwork Orange (1971), with Wendy Carlos’s synthesiser versions.
Mozart’s Eine kleine Nachtmusik (1787) is the tune the priest recognises instantly when the elderly Salieri plays him his own forgotten melodies in Amadeus (1984).
Walter Murphy’s disco “A Fifth of Beethoven”, built on the Fifth Symphony (1808), was a No. 1 hit on the Saturday Night Fever soundtrack (1977).
“La Marseillaise” (1792), France’s anthem, drowns out the German officers’ song in the famous “duel of the anthems” at Rick’s Café in Casablanca (1942).
The medieval chant “Dies irae” (13th century) is the slow, doom-laden line Wendy Carlos and Rachel Elkind built the opening titles of The Shining (1980) on.
Judge Doom taps out “Shave and a Haircut”, a jingle from the 1890s, knowing no toon can resist finishing it with “two bits!” — Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988).
Mykola Leontovych’s Ukrainian “Shchedryk” (1916), known in English as “Carol of the Bells”, rings through the Christmas soundtrack of Home Alone (1990).
The traditional Scottish “Auld Lang Syne” (Burns, 1788) is what the whole town sings around George Bailey at the end of It’s a Wonderful Life (1946).
